name: Executive Order of March 19, 1874 establishing the Walker River Reservation
aka: Walker River Indian Reservation executive order
citation: Executive Order of March 19, 1874 (1 Kappler 869; Royce cession 560)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. President Grant set apart the Walker River Reservation, as surveyed by Eugene Monroe in December 1864, for the use of the Paiute (Royce 560).

The Indian Claims Commission held the reservation was in fact established on November 29, 1859 by Interior Department action, as the United States had itself argued and won in United States v. Walker River Irrigation District, 104 F.2d 334 (9th Cir. 1939).
Under the Winters doctrine, as applied to this reservation in that 1939 case, the reservation carried reserved water from the Walker River.

breaches.what: The Northern Paiute, including the Walker River tribe, pressed claims before the Indian Claims Commission in Docket 87-A that the Commission described as relating to the unlawful taking of reservation lands, unlawful trespasses on their land and conversion of their property. The case was transferred to the Court of Claims in 1978; no finding on these claims was found.

today: The Commission found in Docket 87 that the Paiute lands of western Nevada outside the Pyramid Lake and Walker River reservations were taken without compensation on December 31, 1862, when the two reservations had come into operation, and awarded a net $15,790,000.00 (final judgment, November 4, 1965). That finding concerns the land outside this reservation, so it is recorded here and not counted as a breach of this order. A presidential proclamation of September 26, 1906 opened reservation lands to settlement after allotments under an Act of May 27, 1902; whether the tribe consented was not settled from an opened source.

openQuestions: The 1902 Act and the 1906 opening of the reservation, which took Walker Lake and much of the reservation out of tribal hands according to secondary sources, need a primary source and any finding on consent or compensation.
United States v. Southern Pacific Transportation Co., 543 F.2d 676 (9th Cir. 1976), on the railroad across the reservation, could not be opened.
The outcome of Docket 87-A after its 1978 transfer to the Court of Claims was not found.
The tribe's own history of the reservation was not located; nationVoice is empty for that reason.
